The first account is always compelling — it is told from one perspective, with the natural selection of facts that makes that perspective look right. It is only when the other party speaks that the full complexity of the situation becomes visible. The wisdom implication is practical: suspend judgment until both sides have been heard. The hasty judge who rules for the first speaker is not being decisive; they are being foolish, because they are making a decision with half the available information. This principle applies in marriages, friendships, workplaces, churches — anywhere that two accounts of the same event are in conflict.

verseByVerse.quote: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue… there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother."
verseByVerse.commentary: Verse 21 is the climax of chapter 18's speech ethics: the tongue has the power of death and life. Not merely the power to encourage or discourage, to please or offend — but death and life. This is the strongest possible statement of the stakes involved in every act of speech. James 3:6 elaborates: "the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness… it is a restless evil, full of deadly poison." And yet the same tongue, governed by wisdom and love, can give life. The juxtaposition with verse 24 — "there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother" — invites the christological reading: the one who is the Word, who spoke life into existence (John 1:3), who speaks words of eternal life (John 6:68), is the friend whose tongue brings only life, who is closer than any brother, and whose friendship is the ultimate gift of Wisdom.

18.theology: The theology of speech: death and life in the tongue. Proverbs 18:21 — "death and life are in the power of the tongue" — is the most theologically weighty speech proverb in the book. It grounds the speech ethics of Proverbs not in social convention or reputation management but in the deepest realities of human existence: life and death. This is possible because human beings are made in the image of the God who spoke creation into existence and whose word is the source of all life. When we speak, we are exercising a capacity that reflects our Maker — which means that the misuse of speech is not merely rude or unkind but a distortion of the image of God. And the use of speech to give life — to encourage, to tell the truth, to speak the gospel — is a participation in the creative, life-giving work of the one who is the Word.
18.examples:
Then: "The name of the LORD is a strong tower" (v. 10) was not abstract theology for Israel; it was the daily reality of a nation surrounded by enemies, dependent on God's protection in a way that the great empires were not. The person who ran to the LORD's name was the person who, in the absence of a strong army or a fortified city, had discovered that the LORD himself was stronger than any alternative. The refugee who arrives at the tower breathless and trembling is not demonstrating weakness; they are demonstrating the wisdom that knows where safety actually resides.

Now: "A fool takes no pleasure in understanding, but only in expressing his opinion" (v. 2) has never been more relevant than in the age of social media, where the primary mode of engagement is the public declaration of one's views, and where the discipline of genuine understanding — of reading carefully, listening fully, considering the other perspective — is systematically discouraged by algorithms that reward strong expression over patient comprehension. Keller's observation that wisdom requires the humility to be genuinely interested in understanding applies with particular force to digital discourse: the wisest person in any online conversation is probably the one saying the least.

19.title: Poverty, Wealth, and the LORD
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool. <sup>3</sup>When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD. <sup>11</sup>Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. <sup>14</sup>House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD. <sup>17</sup>Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed. <sup>20</sup>Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future. <sup>21</sup>Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. <sup>23</sup>The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 ranges across poverty and wealth, marriage, generosity to the poor, the sovereignty of God, and the fear of the LORD as the foundation of the satisfied life. It opens with one of Proverbs' "better than" comparisons — the poor person of integrity is better than the foolish person who is crooked in speech — and closes with the settled confidence of the one who fears the LORD: "he will not be visited by harm."

Two of the chapter's most important proverbs address the relationship between human plans and divine purpose (v. 21 — a companion to 16:9) and generosity to the poor (v. 17 — one of the most striking economic proverbs in the book). Verse 17 frames generosity as lending to God himself: the one who is generous to the poor has the LORD as their debtor, and the repayment is guaranteed. This is not a transaction but a theological statement: care for the poor is care for the God who made them and identifies himself with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: One of the most honest and uncomfortable observations in Proverbs. The pattern is universal: we make foolish choices, the choices bring consequences, and we blame God for the consequences. The fool's rage against the LORD is not the rage of the person who has been genuinely wronged by divine injustice; it is the rage of the person who has walked into a wall of their own construction and chosen to accuse the architect rather than the builder. This is the ultimate form of the epistemological foolishness that Proverbs consistently diagnoses: the refusal to acknowledge one's own contribution to one's own difficulties. The beginning of wisdom, in such situations, is to stop raging and start examining — to ask honestly, "how did my own choices contribute to where I am?"

verseByVerse.quote: "House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The proverb distinguishes between two kinds of blessing: the inherited (house and wealth, which come from human agency across generations) and the given (a prudent wife, which comes from the LORD). The distinction is not a denigration of inherited wealth but a recognition that there are goods that no amount of money, strategy, or family connection can secure. A prudent spouse — wise, discerning, trustworthy, of good character — is not a purchasable commodity or an achievable outcome of clever searching; they are a gift. The same recognition appears in the description of the excellent wife in chapter 31: her value is "far above rubies" — beyond the reach of the market. This is Proverbs' way of saying that the most important things in life are received, not achieved.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most theologically audacious proverbs in the book. To give to the poor is to lend to the LORD — with the implication that the LORD is now in the position of a debtor, obligated to repay. The language is deliberately commercial: a loan, a repayment, a debt. The staggering claim is that God himself stands behind the needs of the poor in such a way that meeting those needs is an act directed toward God. Matthew 25:40 confirms the logic from a different angle: "as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me." The poor person is not merely an occasion for charity; they are a site of encounter with God. Generosity to them is an act of faith — trust that the LORD will repay, that the investment made in him through the poor is the most secure investment possible.

verseByVerse.quote: "Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand."
verseByVerse.commentary: The companion proverb to 16:9, and the fullest statement of the sovereignty of God's purposes in Proverbs. Human plans are genuinely many — the mind is fertile, the imagination productive, the ambition expansive. But the LORD's purpose — singular, stable, unfrustrated — stands. Not "eventually stands" or "usually stands" but simply "will stand": it is as certain as the character of the one who purposes it. Isaiah 46:10 makes the same claim from the perspective of prophecy: "my counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose." This is not a counsel to stop planning but a counsel to hold plans loosely, to plan with the open hand of the person who knows that the outcome belongs to the LORD and who is content to receive whatever he establishes.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm."
verseByVerse.commentary: The fear of the LORD is here described not only as the beginning of wisdom (1:7) but as the path to a specific experiential state: resting satisfied, not visited by harm. This does not promise freedom from all difficulty — Proverbs is too realistic for that — but a settled quality of inner life that external circumstances cannot fundamentally disturb. "Rests satisfied" — the person whose life is ordered around the fear of the LORD has found the thing that actually satisfies, and is no longer driven by the restless hunger of the one who seeks satisfaction in things that cannot provide it. Augustine's famous prayer captures this precisely: "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The fear of the LORD is the path to the rest that the heart was created for.

19.theology: The poor, the LORD, and the economics of grace. Proverbs 19:17 — "whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD" — is the wisdom literature's most direct statement of what might be called the economics of grace: the system of exchange that operates in the kingdom of God, where generosity to the vulnerable is generosity to God himself. This is consistent with the theology of the image of God (14:31 — oppressing the poor insults the Maker) and with the prophetic tradition (Amos, Micah, Isaiah — care for the poor is the litmus test of genuine covenant faithfulness). And it is confirmed by Jesus, who in Matthew 25 makes the treatment of the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, and the imprisoned the criterion by which the nations are judged: what is done or not done to the least is done or not done to him. Generosity to the poor is not optional philanthropy; it is covenantal faithfulness to the LORD who identifies himself with them.
19.examples:
Then: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD" (v. 3) was recognisable to every ancient Israelite who had seen the pattern in their own community: the person who made bad decisions (foolish financial risks, sexual unfaithfulness, dishonest dealings) and then, when the consequences arrived, complained that God was being unfair. This is not a modern phenomenon; it is the timeless human instinct to attribute to God what we ourselves have caused. The wisdom tradition's insistence on honest self-examination is the antidote.

Now: "A prudent wife is from the LORD" (v. 14) is the wisdom perspective on the pursuit of a spouse. In a culture that approaches marriage as a matter of personal preference, strategic compatibility, and market dynamics, Proverbs insists that the most important qualities in a spouse — wisdom, character, prudence, faithfulness — are ultimately gifts of God rather than achievements of searching. This does not mean passivity in the search but a posture of dependence and gratitude: the wisdom to recognise a genuine gift when it is offered, and the humility to receive it as from the LORD rather than as a personal achievement.

20.title: Wine Is a Mocker
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise. <sup>5</sup>The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. <sup>7</sup>The righteous who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him! <sup>9</sup>Who can say, "I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin"? <sup>12</sup>The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. <sup>18</sup>Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. <sup>22</sup>Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. <sup>24</sup>A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his own way? <sup>27</sup>The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is one of the more theologically reflective chapters in the Solomonic collection, with several proverbs that press beneath the surface of behaviour to the deeper questions of human nature and divine governance. "Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?" (v. 9) is one of the most important rhetorical questions in the Old Testament — an implicit answer that anticipates the universal sinfulness that Paul will articulate in Romans 3. And "the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts" (v. 27) is a remarkable statement about divine omniscience and human self-knowledge.

The chapter also contains an important observation about deep motivation: "the purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (v. 5). Human motivation is rarely transparent — people do not always know why they do what they do, and neither do the people around them. The person of understanding has the patient, empathetic skill to draw out what is hidden — to hear beneath the stated reason to the actual reason, to see beneath the presenting behaviour to the deeper desire or fear that drives it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise."
verseByVerse.commentary: The personification of wine as a "mocker" — the same term used for the scorner who is Proverbs' most extreme example of folly — is a warning about the nature of intoxication. Wine does not merely relax; it deceives. It promises wisdom and gives foolishness; it promises pleasure and delivers regret; it promises freedom and delivers slavery. The person who is "led astray" by it — who is mastered by what they thought they were mastering — is, by Proverbs' definition, not wise. This is not an absolute prohibition of alcohol (Proverbs and the wider Old Testament do not teach that) but a warning about the specific danger of being led astray by anything that promises what only the fear of the LORD can deliver: genuine wisdom, genuine joy, genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out."
verseByVerse.commentary: The image of deep water for the hidden purposes of the human heart is illuminating: deep water is not easily accessible, not visible from the surface, and requires deliberate effort to reach. The counsellor, the pastor, the wise friend who can draw out what is hidden — who can ask the right question, create the right atmosphere of trust, and receive what surfaces without alarm or judgment — is performing one of the most valuable human services. This is not manipulation or extraction against the will; it is the patient, empathetic skill of creating the conditions in which what is genuinely present can emerge. Jesus' conversations with Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, and the rich young ruler are all examples of this kind of drawing out: asking the question that reaches the deep water of the heart's real question.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The rhetorical question expects the answer: no one. This is the wisdom literature's most explicit statement of the universal sinfulness of humanity — the recognition that self-righteousness is always a delusion, that no human being can truthfully claim to have achieved a clean heart or pure life by their own efforts. The implication is profound: if no one can clean their own heart, then the clean heart must come from somewhere else. The gospel is the answer Proverbs anticipates but cannot yet fully articulate: the one who creates in us a clean heart (Ps 51:10) is the God who gives a new heart and a new spirit (Ezek 36:26), who cleanses from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9) through the blood of the one who had no sin of his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not say, 'I will repay evil'; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The command against personal vengeance is grounded in trust in the LORD as the ultimate agent of justice. "Wait for the LORD" — the person who trusts the LORD with justice is freed from the exhausting and corrupting project of managing their own revenge. This is Paul's direct application in Romans 12:19: "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.'" The person who waits for the LORD is not passive; they are actively trusting a more reliable agent of justice than themselves. And in the waiting, they are freed from the bitterness and corruption that the project of revenge always produces in those who pursue it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most mysterious and profound proverbs in the book. The human spirit — the innermost self, the faculty of self-awareness and moral perception — is described as the LORD's lamp: the instrument by which he illuminates the hidden depths of the human person. This anticipates the New Testament teaching on the Spirit's role in conviction, sanctification, and illumination: the Spirit of God searches the depths of God (1 Cor 2:10–11) and also searches the depths of the human heart, revealing what is hidden, exposing what is false, and making known what is true. The human capacity for self-knowledge — conscience, moral awareness, the sense of guilt and the aspiration toward goodness — is not merely a psychological function but a divine gift, the lamp that God has lit within the human being to illuminate what is there.

20.theology: Universal sinfulness and the need for divine cleansing. Proverbs 20:9 — "who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?" — is the wisdom literature's contribution to the biblical theology of universal human sinfulness. The rhetorical question's implied answer (no one) is the foundation for the entire New Testament soteriology: if no one can clean their own heart, then the gospel's offer of cleansing through Christ is not a luxury for the morally sensitive but a necessity for every human being. Keller reads Proverbs 20:9 as the point at which the wisdom tradition's self-knowledge leads inevitably to the need for grace: the wise person, who has genuinely attended to the reality of their own heart, discovers what Jeremiah 17:9 states explicitly ("the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick — who can understand it?") — and this discovery is the beginning of the openness to the gospel.
20.examples:
Then: "The righteous who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him!" (v. 7) is the multigenerational vision of wisdom: the blessing of integrity is not merely personal but propagates to the next generation. The children of the person of integrity grow up in an environment shaped by that integrity — they observe it, absorb it, are formed by it. This is not a guarantee of their own righteousness (each person must make their own choices) but a recognition that the environment of integrity is itself a gift to the next generation, one of the most important things a parent can provide.

Now: "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (v. 5) is the wisdom text for all pastoral and counselling ministry. The presenting question is rarely the real question; the stated reason for the decision is rarely the deepest reason; the surface behaviour is rarely the whole story. The person of understanding — who has learned to listen patiently, to ask the question beneath the question, to create the trust that allows the deep water to surface — is one of the most valuable people any community can have. This is pastoral wisdom as Proverbs understands it: not the rapid dispensing of advice but the patient, empathetic drawing out of what is genuinely there.

21.title: The King's Heart
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. <sup>2</sup>Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart. <sup>3</sup>To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. <sup>5</sup>The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. <sup>13</sup>Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. <sup>21</sup>Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor. <sup>23</sup>Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. <sup>30</sup>No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. <sup>31</sup>The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 opens with the most striking statement of divine sovereignty in the book: "the king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will" (v. 1). If the most powerful human being — the king, whose word is law — is in the LORD's hands as easily as a stream of water, then no human power or human plan can ultimately resist the purposes of God. The chapter closes with the companion proverb: "the horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD" (v. 31). Between the king's heart and the battle horse, human agency and divine sovereignty bracket the entire chapter.

The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most important social ethics proverbs: "whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered" (v. 13). The connection between our response to others' need and God's response to our need is stated here with stark symmetry: those who do not hear the cry of the poor will not be heard when they cry. This is the justice principle of reciprocity that runs through the entire wisdom tradition and that Jesus will make explicit: "with the measure you use it will be measured to you" (Matt 7:2).

verseByVerse.quote: "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will."
verseByVerse.commentary: The image of the irrigation channel is precise: the farmer who controls where the water flows controls where the crops grow. The stream goes where the channel directs it, without resistance, without volition. The king's heart — the most powerful human will in any ancient society — is in the LORD's hands with the same ease. This does not mean that kings are puppets without genuine agency (Proverbs consistently addresses them as responsible moral agents); it means that the outcomes of their decisions are in the LORD's governance. Pharaoh plans to destroy Israel; his plans become the occasion for the Exodus. Cyrus plans to expand his empire; his plans become the instrument of Israel's restoration (Isa 44:28). The mighty are turned by the one who is mightier, without their knowledge and without violence to their will.

verseByVerse.quote: "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice."
verseByVerse.commentary: This proverb stands in the tradition of the great prophetic critiques of empty religion (1 Sam 15:22; Isa 1:11–17; Mic 6:6–8; Hos 6:6). Sacrifice — the most important religious act in the ancient world — is less acceptable to the LORD than righteousness and justice in everyday life. The God who is himself righteous and just (Deut 32:4) is more pleased by the reflection of his character in human conduct than by ritual acts that are disconnected from character. This does not eliminate sacrifice (which in the Old Testament is divinely commanded) but relativises it: sacrifice without justice is unacceptable; justice without sacrifice may be more acceptable than sacrifice without justice. Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 twice (Matt 9:13; 12:7) to make the same point: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered."
verseByVerse.commentary: The reciprocity is exact and sobering: the closed ear becomes the unanswered cry. The person who has the resources to help and the awareness of need, and who deliberately closes their ear, has chosen a posture toward need that will be reflected in the LORD's posture toward their own need. This is not a mechanical transaction but a description of the character-consequence relationship that runs through Proverbs: the person who has developed the habit of not hearing the poor has, in the process, formed a character that is deaf to genuine need — including the need that will eventually be their own. And the God who hears the cry of the poor (Ps 9:18; 34:6) does not hear the cry of those who do not hear the poor. James 2:13 makes the same connection: "judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy."

verseByVerse.quote: "No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The two closing proverbs of the chapter are the book's most comprehensive statement of divine sovereignty over human wisdom and human power. No wisdom — however brilliant; no understanding — however acute; no counsel — however strategically sophisticated — can ultimately prevail against the LORD's purposes. And no military preparation — however thorough; no horse — however well-trained — can secure the victory. Psalm 33:16–17 says the same: "the king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength. The war horse is a false hope for salvation." The appropriate response is not passivity but the humble, grateful recognition that all ultimate security rests not in what we have prepared but in whom we trust.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor."
verseByVerse.commentary: The pursuit of righteousness and kindness (hesed — steadfast love, covenant faithfulness) leads to life, righteousness, and honour — an abundance of what was sought and more besides. This is the wisdom principle of seeking the right thing: the person who pursues the intrinsic goods of character and relationship finds them, plus the extrinsic goods (honour, life) that cannot be obtained by direct pursuit. It is a specific application of the kingdom principle that Jesus articulates: "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you" (Matt 6:33). The things that matter most — life, righteousness, honour in the deepest sense — are found by those who pursue what actually produces them: the character of God reflected in human life.

21.theology: Divine sovereignty over history and the limits of human power. Proverbs 21:1 and 21:30–31 together form the book's most comprehensive statement of divine sovereignty over history. The king's heart, the counsellor's wisdom, the warrior's horse — all are in the LORD's hands. This is not a counsel of fatalism but of faith: the person who knows that the LORD governs the king's heart and secures the victory is freed from the anxiety of ultimate responsibility. They plan, they prepare, they fight — but they hold the outcome loosely, because they know who holds the outcome. This is the Calvinist tradition's "God controls and we are responsible" applied to the full range of human endeavour: political, intellectual, and military. Human agency is real and matters; but it operates within a governance that ensures the LORD's purposes will stand (19:21).
21.examples:
Then: "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice" (v. 3) was a prophetic challenge to a culture that had learned to separate religious observance from social ethics. The person who offered elaborate sacrifices at the temple while oppressing workers, cheating in business, and ignoring the poor had not understood either sacrifice or justice. The sacrifice is the expression of a life; when the life contradicts the sacrifice, the sacrifice is worse than useless — it is an insult to the God whose character it claims to honour.

Now: "The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD" (v. 31) is the wisdom text for every leader, strategist, and planner who has done everything right and still found the outcome out of their hands. Prepare thoroughly — this is wisdom's consistent counsel. But hold the preparation with an open hand, knowing that the victory is the LORD's to give or withhold according to purposes that exceed your strategy. The leader who has internalised this is both more diligent (because preparation is real responsibility) and more peaceful (because the outcome is not ultimately their burden to carry).

22.title: A Good Name
22.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. <sup>2</sup>The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all. <sup>3</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. <sup>4</sup>The reward of humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. <sup>6</sup>Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. <sup>7</sup>The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. <sup>9</sup>Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. <sup>17</sup>Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge, <sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, <sup>23</sup>for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them. <sup>29</sup>Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 opens the collection's most famous verse — "a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (v.1) — and then pivots to "the thirty sayings of the wise" (vv.17–24:22), a section with remarkable parallels to the Egyptian wisdom text Instruction of Amenemope. That such wisdom appeared across cultures does not diminish Scripture; it shows that general revelation seeds wisdom broadly, while special revelation perfects and redeems it.

The chapter holds together two great themes: reputation rightly ordered (vv.1–9) and instruction rightly received (vv.17–29). A good name is not a brand to manage but a life poured out in integrity before God. The rich and poor alike bear the LORD's image (v.2) — a leveling that should dismantle both pride and contempt.

Timothy Keller notes that "fear of the LORD" (v.4) is the engine beneath all genuine wisdom. Humility before God produces the kind of person whose name becomes, almost accidentally, a good one. The one who grasps for reputation loses it; the one who fears God gains it freely.

verseByVerse.quote: "A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A good name" in the ancient world meant character that generated lasting trust — the kind of reputation that survived death and blessed one's children. This is not image management; it is a life of integrity. Proverbs relentlessly exposes the fool's attempt to shortcut reputation through wealth or cleverness. Only the fear of the LORD builds a name that endures.

Keller observes that Jesus is the one whose name is above every name (Phil. 2:9) — not because he grasped it, but because he emptied himself. Christian ambition, then, is paradoxically shaped by downward mobility: the name that matters most is found in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the maker of them all."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of Proverbs' most socially subversive lines. In the ancient Near East, wealth signaled divine favor and poverty divine curse. Proverbs demolishes that equation. The LORD made both; class distinctions are penultimate. This verse does not flatten economics but refuses to let economics determine dignity. The church is the community where this truth is embodied — where the powerful and the marginalized share bread at the same table.

verseByVerse.quote: "Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it."
verseByVerse.commentary: Perhaps the most quoted parenting verse in Proverbs. "The way he should go" carries the Hebrew idiom al-pi darko — literally "according to his way," which may include his natural bent and giftedness, not just doctrinal content. Formation is holistic: habits, worship rhythms, the texture of daily life oriented toward God. Proverbs does not promise mechanical results — children are moral agents — but wisdom-shaped homes produce deeply rooted people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, for the LORD will plead their cause."
verseByVerse.commentary: "The gate" was the civic and commercial center where justice was administered. To crush the poor there was to corrupt the very mechanism meant to protect them. Proverbs is unambiguous: economic injustice is not merely a social problem — it is a theological one. The LORD himself becomes the plaintiff (v.23). The gospel intensifies this: Christ, who was poor for our sakes (2 Cor. 8:9), identifies with the crushed. Justice for the poor is never optional in wisdom literature.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings."
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs dignifies ordinary work. Skillfulness — mahir, swift, practiced, expert — is the mark of the person who takes their calling seriously before God. The doctrine of vocation holds that all legitimate work done faithfully is an act of worship. The artisan, the scribe, the farmer, the merchant — each can stand before kings, not because they are ambitious, but because they have served well. Excellence flows from loving the work God gave you, not from career calculation.

22.theology:
The LORD as Maker of Rich and Poor. Verse 2 is theologically dense. To say that the LORD made both rich and poor is not to endorse economic inequality as divinely ordained but to strip class of ultimate significance. Both are equally creatures, equally sinners, equally in need of grace. Christian theology presses further: both are equally candidates for redemption, equally called to table fellowship. The cross is the great leveling — "there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free" (Gal. 3:28).

Humility and the Fear of the LORD (v.4). Proverbs keeps returning to this pair. Humility is not self-deprecation; it is accurate sight — seeing oneself as creature before Creator. The fear of the LORD is the relational disposition that keeps that sight clear. Together they produce a life of remarkable freedom: freed from status anxiety, freed from the grasping that destroys the soul. "Riches and honor and life" are given, not seized.
22.examples:
Then: Israelite parents would teach children in the rhythms of daily life — working, eating, traveling (Deut. 6:7). The craftsman's workshop was also a school of character. The "gate" was where elders like Boaz administered justice publicly (Ruth 4:1). Chapter 22's advice was entirely practical for a society where reputation, work quality, and economic justice were intertwined in visible community life.

Now: In an age of curated digital personas, "a good name" (v.1) has never been more misunderstood. The proverb cuts against impression management — the good name Proverbs values cannot be manufactured online. Verse 6 speaks to parents worried their children will abandon the faith: wisdom-shaped formation is deeper than we know, even when the season of apparent departure is long. And verses 22–23 call the church to advocate concretely for economic justice — not as political performance, but as the natural overflow of fearing the God who defends the poor.

23.title: Do Not Wear Yourself Out to Get Rich
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, <sup>4</sup>Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. <sup>5</sup>When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven. <sup>6</sup>Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies, <sup>10</sup>Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, <sup>11</sup>for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you. <sup>17</sup>Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. <sup>18</sup>Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off. <sup>19</sup>Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. <sup>22</sup>Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old. <sup>23</sup>Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding. <sup>29</sup>Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? <sup>30</sup>Those who tarry long over wine, those who go to try mixed wine. <sup>33</sup>Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things.
23.overview:
Chapter 23 is a series of urgent parental instructions addressing three great idols: wealth, food and pleasure, and intoxication. The framing device — a son being warned before a meal with a ruler (vv.1–3) and warned again before wine (vv.29–35) — is deliberate. What we eat and drink, and with whom, shapes character more than we imagine.

The center of the chapter is a pair of commands that belong together: "Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off" (vv.17–18). The antidote to the fool's prosperity is not resignation but eschatological confidence — a hope rooted in the character of God, not the circumstances of the moment.

Keller reads verse 23 — "Buy truth, and do not sell it" — as the heart of the chapter. Truth is not a commodity; it is a person (John 14:6). The wisdom tradition points toward One whose price was infinite and whose gift is freely given.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary: One of Proverbs' sharpest observations about wealth: it is ontologically unstable. The image of money sprouting eagle's wings is both comic and serious — wealth has the capacity to vanish precisely when it seems most secure. The fool is the one who builds a life around something that cannot hold weight. This is not an argument for poverty but for appropriate detachment: work faithfully, hold wealth loosely, fear the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The "Redeemer" (goel) is the kinsman-redeemer — the family member obligated to rescue and restore what was lost. Applied to God, it means the fatherless are not unprotected; the LORD himself stands in the place of their absent defender. This is one of the Old Testament's most tender images of divine advocacy. The gospel crowns it: our great Redeemer paid the debt we could not pay (Ruth 4 → Boaz as type; Christ as antitype).

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the theological heart of the chapter and one of Proverbs' richest pastoral texts. Envy of the wicked is not merely a feeling problem but a sight problem — we are only seeing the present. The fear of the LORD opens the eye to "a future" (acharit) — an end, a culmination. The wicked have prosperity now but no future; the righteous may struggle now but their hope is not cut off. This is precisely the argument of Psalm 73, and it points toward resurrection: the final chapter has not been written.

verseByVerse.quote: "Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding."
verseByVerse.commentary: The command to "buy truth" is striking — as if truth were a commodity in the marketplace. The point is that truth costs something: comfort, convenience, pride, reputation. But unlike money, truth must never be sold. You may have to give something up to receive it; you must never trade it away for something lesser. Jesus said "the truth will set you free" (John 8:32) — but he also said "I am the truth" (John 14:6). To buy truth is, ultimately, to come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who has woe? Who has sorrow?... Those who tarry long over wine... Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things."
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs' famous meditation on drunkenness is not mere temperance lecturing. It traces the anatomy of addiction: the initial pleasure, the creeping domination, the distorted perception, the perverse speech, the inability to stop. "When shall I awake? I must have another drink" (v.35) is one of the Bible's most candid portrayals of a disordered appetite. Wine is a gift (Psalm 104:15), but any good gift becomes tyrannical when it displaces the fear of the LORD. The path to freedom runs through One who said "I am the vine" — the true source of joy that does not destroy.

23.theology:
The God Who Redeems. The title goel (v.11) is loaded with covenantal meaning. Ruth's story turns on it; Isaiah uses it for God's redemption of Israel from exile (Isa. 41:14; 43:14); the New Testament sees Christ as the ultimate Redeemer who pays the price no family member could afford. That God is the Redeemer of the fatherless means no one is truly without a defender — which is why the church must embody that advocacy in concrete, particular acts of care.

Eschatological Hope as Wisdom. Verses 17–18 show that wisdom is inseparable from eschatology. To fear the LORD is to orient yourself toward a future guaranteed by the character of God, not by present circumstances. This is not optimism (a temperamental preference for good outcomes) but hope (a theologically grounded confidence in the One who controls the end). The resurrection of Jesus is the anchor of that hope — "your hope will not be cut off" because death itself was cut off at the cross.
23.examples:
Then: A meal with a ruler in the ancient world was a political event — gifts and flattery were expected. The son is warned to see past the knife at his throat and not lose himself to ambitious social climbing (vv.1–3). Landmark boundaries were sacrosanct in Israelite law (Deut. 19:14); moving them was theft dressed as nothing. The wine section (vv.29–35) addressed a culture where wine was the primary social lubricant — wisdom does not prohibit it but demands mastery over it.

Now: The wealth section (vv.4–5) speaks directly to the professional-class anxiety that drives overwork and portfolio obsession. The eschatological correction (vv.17–18) is the only real cure for envy of the successful fool: a longer view. And the wine section remains searingly contemporary — addiction affects every demographic, and Proverbs' anatomical description of it is more clinical than moralistic. The gospel adds to wisdom's diagnosis: the heart craves what only God can give, and the disordered craving for any substance is finally a spiritual hunger misdirected.

24.title: Do Not Envy the Wicked
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, <sup>2</sup>for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble. <sup>3</sup>By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; <sup>4</sup>by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches. <sup>10</sup>If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. <sup>11</sup>Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. <sup>13</sup>My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. <sup>14</sup>Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off. <sup>16</sup>for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in calamity. <sup>17</sup>Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, <sup>19</sup>Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, <sup>20</sup>for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out. <sup>29</sup>Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."
24.overview:
Chapter 24 returns to the theme of envy with fresh urgency (vv.1, 19–20) and surrounds it with wisdom's great affirmations: the wisdom-built house (vv.3–4), the resilience of the righteous (v.16), the warning against schadenfreude (v.17), and the sweetness of wisdom itself (vv.13–14). The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most striking ethical demands: rescue those being led to slaughter (vv.11–12), with the sobering reminder that pleading ignorance before the God who weighs hearts will not stand.

The key structural move is the contrast between two futures. The wicked may prosper now, but "the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out" (v.20). Wisdom sees what is coming. The righteous, by contrast, may fall repeatedly — but they rise (v.16). Resurrection hope is embedded in Proverbs' anthropology long before Easter morning.

verseByVerse.quote: "By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches."
verseByVerse.commentary: The "house" here is simultaneously a family, a home, a legacy, and a life. Proverbs consistently uses architectural language for the work of wisdom: building, establishing, filling. This is wisdom as constructive power, not merely corrective — it does not only keep you from folly but actively builds something beautiful. In the New Testament, Christ is the wise builder who constructs his church on the rock (Matt. 7:24–27; 1 Cor. 3:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: "Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter."
verseByVerse.commentary: This text has haunted readers throughout history, including during the Holocaust, when "pleading ignorance" was precisely the excuse many offered. Proverbs will not allow it: God weighs the heart, and he knows when knowledge was available (v.12). The demand is not merely legal but deeply moral — wisdom perceives injustice and acts. The Christian reads this in light of Christ, who rescued those being taken to death by giving himself in their place, and now sends his people as agents of that rescue mission.

verseByVerse.quote: "My son, eat honey, for it is good... Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off."
verseByVerse.commentary: The honey analogy is Proverbs' invitation to taste wisdom as a pleasure, not merely a duty. Wisdom is not bitter medicine; it is intrinsically delicious to those whose palates are trained by the fear of the LORD. The Psalmist agrees: "How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Ps. 119:103). The gospel deepens this: Christ is the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden (Col. 2:3) — to know him is to taste the sweetest wisdom of all.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in calamity."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Seven times" is not a precise count but a Hebrew idiom for completeness — no matter how many times. The righteous person is not one who never falls but one who gets up, because their rising is grounded in the LORD who raises. This verse distinguishes failure from destruction: the righteous can fail without being finished. The wicked stumble and that stumble is final, not because God is cruel, but because they have built on nothing. For the Christian, verse 16 is resurrection logic applied to daily life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles."
verseByVerse.commentary: Schadenfreude — pleasure at the suffering of one's enemy — is one of the most natural and most corrosive of human impulses. Proverbs bans it not only because it is unseemly but because it signals a heart that has made the enemy's defeat its god. The one who rejoices at an enemy's fall has confused justice with vengeance. Jesus sharpens this: "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (Matt. 5:44). The cross is the ultimate anti-schadenfreude — Christ rejoiced in the salvation of his enemies, even at infinite cost.

24.theology:
Resurrection Anthropology. Verse 16 embeds a proto-resurrection hope in Proverbs' account of the righteous life. The righteous are not those who are immune to falling but those who are constitutionally oriented toward rising — because the God they fear is the God who raises the dead. Paul develops this in 2 Cor. 4:9: "struck down, but not destroyed." The wicked have no such resource; their stumble in calamity is final because they have no one to raise them.

The Ethics of Rescue. Verses 11–12 establish that wisdom is not passive. Knowing and not acting is its own form of guilt. This anticipates the prophetic tradition (Isa. 1:17; Micah 6:8) and the New Testament (James 1:27). The God who weighs hearts is not fooled by performative ignorance. The church that knows about injustice and does nothing has not yet grasped the wisdom of God.
24.examples:
Then: The "rescue" command (vv.11–12) likely referred to specific situations: wrongful capital punishment at the gate, debt slavery, or unjust judicial proceedings. Witnesses could intervene, elders could speak. "Pleading ignorance" was already a known excuse. The honey metaphor (v.13) connected wisdom to the agricultural bounty of Canaan — wisdom is as Israelite as the honey of the promised land.

Now: Verse 16 is a lifeline for any Christian in a season of repeated failure — addiction recovery, pastoral burnout, protracted grief, marital crisis. The righteous person is not the one who falls least but the one who keeps getting up. Verses 11–12 speak to every generation that faces systemic injustice: the question is always whether those who know will act. And verse 17 confronts social-media culture's delight in public shaming and the downfall of enemies — wisdom calls for a different emotional posture toward those who fail, even those who harmed us.

25.title: A Word Fitly Spoken
25.text: <sup>1</sup>These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied. <sup>2</sup>It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out. <sup>6</sup>Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, <sup>11</sup>A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver. <sup>13</sup>Like the cold of snow in harvest time is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters. <sup>15</sup>With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone. <sup>16</sup>If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. <sup>20</sup>Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda. <sup>21</sup>If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, <sup>22</sup>for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you. <sup>25</sup>Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 opens the Hezekiah collection (chapters 25–29), proverbs copied and arranged by the scribes of King Hezekiah around 700 B.C. The chapter is particularly rich in extended similes — a literary hallmark. Where many proverbs state a truth flatly, chapter 25 paints it: apples of gold, cold snow in harvest, a soft tongue breaking bone.

The organizing theme is speech — what it is, what it can do, and how precious it is when used well. A word fitly spoken (v.11) is not merely pleasant; it is a work of art that reflects the beauty of wisdom itself. Speech is also powerful: a soft tongue breaks bone (v.15), meaning patient persuasion accomplishes what force cannot.

The ethical climax is verses 21–22: give bread to your enemy. Paul quotes this in Romans 12:20, embedding it in his great vision of non-retaliation and love. What Proverbs presents as wisdom, Paul presents as the shape of cruciform love — the pattern of a community that does not overcome evil with evil but with good.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out."
verseByVerse.commentary: God's concealment is not deception but the dignity of mystery — the universe has depths that reward patient investigation. Human searching is itself a form of worship, a reflection of the image-bearing capacity for rational inquiry. This verse undergirds the Christian tradition's embrace of science and scholarship: to search out what God has hidden is to honor the Hider. The fear of the LORD does not shut down inquiry; it ignites it.

verseByVerse.quote: "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Fitly spoken" — al-ofanav, on its wheels, in its proper situation — suggests a word that arrives at exactly the right moment in exactly the right form. Such a word is rare and valuable: apples of gold in a silver setting, a piece of jewelry where two precious materials mutually enhance each other. Most words are adequate; the fitly spoken word is art. It requires knowledge of the person, sensitivity to the moment, and the patience not to speak before the word is ready. James captures this: "quick to listen, slow to speak" (1:19).

verseByVerse.quote: "If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it."
verseByVerse.commentary: Moderation is not puritanism; it is the condition for continued enjoyment. The person who gorges on honey destroys the very pleasure they sought. Proverbs applies this principle everywhere: food, wine, sleep, sex, even friendship (v.17). The fall into excess always begins with a good thing taken too far. Augustine's formulation is Proverbs' own: our hearts are restless until they rest in God — and only the one whose deepest hunger is satisfied in God can enjoy lesser goods without being consumed by them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda."
verseByVerse.commentary: A verse about the pastoral failure of inappropriate cheerfulness. The one who sings to a grieving heart means well but causes harm — stripping the sufferer of the warmth they needed, causing a caustic reaction. Lament must be received as lament. Job's friends sat silently for seven days (Job 2:13) — when they began to speak, they failed him. The wise counselor reads the room and gives what the moment requires: presence before platitude, tears before songs.

verseByVerse.quote: "If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat... for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Burning coals on his head" is likely a positive image drawn from Egyptian ritual — coals carried on the head as a sign of penitence and shame. The act of giving bread to your enemy does not merely humiliate him; it creates the conditions in which shame can become repentance. Paul cites this in Romans 12:20, between the commands not to repay evil for evil and to overcome evil with good. The Christian reads it christologically: Jesus fed and healed his enemies; the cross is the ultimate burning coal, the act of love so unexpected it breaks the cycle of retaliation.

25.theology:
The Theology of Speech. Proverbs 25 presents speech as one of the central moral acts of human existence. The fitly spoken word (v.11), the faithful messenger (v.13), the soft tongue (v.15), the inappropriate song (v.20) — each is a form of power, either rightly or wrongly exercised. The New Testament elevates this: the Word became flesh (John 1:14), and the Spirit is given to fill our speech with wisdom. Speech is not merely communication; it is the primary medium of love and harm.

Cruciform Ethics. Verses 21–22 anticipate the Sermon on the Mount and Romans 12. Proverbs is not merely a book of prudential advice; it contains an ethics of enemy-love rooted in God's own character. The LORD rewards the one who feeds the enemy (v.22b), confirming that this is not merely clever strategy but a reflection of divine generosity — a God who causes his sun to rise on evil and good alike (Matt. 5:45).
25.examples:
Then: The Hezekiah scribal collection reflects a royal court that valued the art of persuasion and the discipline of speech. Ambassadors, advisors, and court officials lived or died by their words. The apples-of-gold image (v.11) suggests the aesthetic dimensions of wisdom that Israelite court culture cultivated. Verse 25's "good news from a far country" may have evoked the joy of a merchant's return or a military dispatch — news that changed everything.

Now: The pastoral word of verse 20 indicts the relentless positivity that refuses to make room for grief. Grief communities, cancer wards, and counseling rooms require the wisdom to be quiet when songs are wrong and to speak when silence has run its course. Verses 21–22 have a direct application in the age of social media retaliation and culture-war contempt: feeding the enemy is not weakness but the most subversive act available to the Christian. It reclaims the narrative from the logic of revenge.

26.title: Like a Dog Returns to Its Vomit
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool. <sup>2</sup>Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight. <sup>4</sup>Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. <sup>5</sup>Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. <sup>11</sup>Like a dog that returns to its vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. <sup>12</sup>Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. <sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!" <sup>17</sup>Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears. <sup>20</sup>For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. <sup>26</sup>though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly. <sup>28</sup>A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
26.overview:
Chapter 26 is Proverbs' extended anatomy of foolishness, containing the book's most sustained portrait of three types: the fool (vv.1–12), the sluggard (vv.13–16), and the quarrelsome gossip (vv.17–28). It is the longest concentrated treatment of folly in the Bible, and it is written with a sharp, almost satirical wit.

The famous contradiction of verses 4–5 — "Answer not a fool... Answer a fool" — is deliberate. It is not an error but wisdom's acknowledgment that no single rule fits every case. Sometimes engaging a fool drags you down to his level; sometimes silence leaves him unchallenged in his self-delusion. The wise person reads the situation and responds accordingly. This is wisdom's practical epistemology: principles must be applied with judgment, not mechanical rule-following.

The chapter closes with the liar and flatterer (vv.23–28) — people whose words are weapons disguised as gifts. The hidden hatred will eventually be exposed (v.26). Proverbs consistently returns to this: truth is the ultimate victor because God, who is truth, governs history.

verseByVerse.quote: "Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool."
verseByVerse.commentary: Snow in summer and rain at harvest are not merely unseasonable — they are destructive. Honor given to a fool does not merely fail to benefit him; it harms the community by distorting its sense of what deserves recognition. A culture that honors foolishness will eventually be shaped by it. This is a warning to those who confer recognition and platform: the social consequences of misplaced honor are real and lasting.

verseByVerse.quote: "Answer not a fool according to his folly... Answer a fool according to his folly."
verseByVerse.commentary: The deliberate juxtaposition is wisdom's way of refusing to be reduced to an algorithm. There is no single right response to the fool: sometimes engagement dignifies his nonsense; sometimes silence emboldens his self-deception. The wise person must develop the judgment to read which situation calls for which response. This is why wisdom cannot be reduced to a checklist — it requires the formation of character that perceives correctly before it acts. The Pharisees demanded algorithmic answers from Jesus; he answered differently each time because he read each questioner perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Like a dog that returns to its vomit is a fool who repeats his folly."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter quotes this verse in 2 Peter 2:22 in his description of false teachers who return to the corruption they had apparently escaped. The image is viscerally accurate: the return to folly is not a single dramatic act but a sad compulsion, a gravity that pulls the undisciplined person back toward what destroyed them before. Proverbs diagnoses this as a structural feature of foolishness: the fool has not changed the orientation of his heart, so he returns to its natural products. Only reorientation — the fear of the LORD — breaks the cycle.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The self-deceived wise man is more dangerous than the acknowledged fool, because he cannot receive correction. The fool at least knows something is wrong; the man wise in his own eyes has built a closed system that filters out any challenge. Pride is the meta-folly — the folly that prevents all other folly from being seen and addressed. Paul identifies this as the root of pagan darkness: "claiming to be wise, they became fools" (Rom. 1:22). The antidote is the fear of the LORD — an orientation toward one wiser than yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: "For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases."
verseByVerse.commentary: Gossip is fuel. Conflicts that seem to burn with their own energy are almost always maintained by the repeated addition of whispered reports, selective interpretations, and private grievances broadcast sideways. The practical wisdom is simple: stop feeding the fire. The Christian community is called to be a place where gossip starves — not through enforcement but through transformed speech habits. What fuels the fire in a community is most often what its members choose to say to one another about one another.

26.theology:
The Anatomy of Folly. Chapter 26 shows that folly is not a single trait but a complex of related failures: the misallocation of honor (vv.1–3), the inability to learn (v.11), the closed-loop self-confidence (v.12), the laziness that rationalizes itself (vv.13–16), and the tongue used as weapon (vv.17–28). These are not unrelated vices but expressions of the one root: life lived as if God does not exist, with the self as the final reference point. Keller's insight is that the fool is the secularist — not necessarily the atheist, but the one who functionally excludes God from practical decisions.

Self-Deception and Grace. The man wise in his own eyes (v.12) is the hardest case because he is impervious to correction. The gospel's answer is not better argument but encounter with the living God — the experience that brought Isaiah to his knees ("Woe is me!") and Paul to the Damascus road. Conversion is the radical undoing of self-deception, and it is entirely a work of grace.
26.examples:
Then: Court politics made the sluggard (vv.13–16) a recognizable type — the official who invented elaborate reasons for inaction. The whisperer (v.20) operated in every ancient institution, and Proverbs knew that political conflict was usually sustained by informers and gossips, not by genuine grievances alone. The honor-for-fools warning (v.1) addressed a patronage culture where rulers could elevate incompetent favorites with destructive results.

Now: The social media age has made the man wise in his own eyes (v.12) ubiquitous — the confident amateur whose Dunning-Kruger blindness is now amplified to thousands. Verse 20 is a direct diagnosis of online conflict: Twitter feuds, church splits, and family estrangements are almost always sustained by whisperers adding wood. The vv.4–5 tension about answering the fool is the daily dilemma of anyone with a public platform: engaging every foolish take validates it; ignoring every challenge abandons truth. Wisdom, not a rule, is required.

27.title: Do Not Boast About Tomorrow
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. <sup>2</sup>Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. <sup>5</sup>Better is open rebuke than hidden love. <sup>6</sup>Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of a flatterer. <sup>9</sup>Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. <sup>12</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. <sup>17</sup>Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. <sup>19</sup>As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. <sup>20</sup>Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man. <sup>21</sup>The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. <sup>23</sup>Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, <sup>27</sup>There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 is one of Proverbs' warmest chapters, centering on the gifts of genuine friendship (vv.5–10, 17) while bookending with humility about the future (v.1) and the discipline of faithful work (vv.23–27). The famous verse — "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (v.17) — is embedded in a larger account of what makes friendship transformative rather than merely pleasant.

The chapter distinguishes sharply between the flatterer and the faithful friend. Flattery gives kisses; friendship gives wounds. The wound of a friend is painful but constructive — it is love that refuses to leave you in your blind spots. The flatterer's kisses are pleasant but corrosive, feeding the self-deception that Proverbs constantly diagnoses as the root of folly.

The closing pastoral image (vv.23–27) is often overlooked: the wise man tends his flocks attentively, knowing that wealth is temporary and natural abundance cycles. This is wisdom applied to economics — attention, stewardship, patience. It is a far cry from the "riches sprout wings" speculation of the fool.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring."
verseByVerse.commentary: James cites this verse almost verbatim (James 4:13–14), applying it to businessmen who plan without reference to the Lord's will. The point is not that planning is wrong but that boasting about tomorrow is a claim to sovereignty you do not have. The humble planner says "if the Lord wills" (James 4:15). The fear of the LORD produces a certain lightness about the future — not fatalism, but trust that releases the grip of anxiety. Tomorrow belongs to the One who holds all days.

verseByVerse.quote: "Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of a flatterer."
verseByVerse.commentary: Hidden love is not love in any meaningful sense — it is affection that fails its object at the crucial moment. Open rebuke is frightening but life-giving. The "wounds of a friend" are the corrective conversations that require more courage than any physical confrontation. Every serious Christian needs at least one person who will tell them what they do not want to hear. The flatterer's kisses feel better but leave you more deeply lost. Nathan's rebuke of David (2 Sam. 12) is the biblical paradigm: one faithful wound that saved a soul.

verseByVerse.quote: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another."
verseByVerse.commentary: Iron sharpens iron through friction — contact that would damage softer materials produces an edge in iron. Genuine friendship is not smooth and comfortable; it involves the friction of two different people with different perspectives pressing against each other. The result is sharpness — precision, clarity, readiness. This is why the church is not optional for Christian formation: the isolated Christian does not get sharpened. We need the friction of genuine community to become who God is calling us to be.

verseByVerse.quote: "As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man."
verseByVerse.commentary: The heart is the truest mirror of who a person is. What you love, fear, and worship ultimately shows — not in occasional performances but in the whole pattern of a life. Jeremiah diagnosed the heart as "deceitful above all things" (Jer. 17:9) — it hides even from its owner. But the Spirit illuminates, and community (see vv.5–6, 17) makes visible what the heart has been concealing. The examined life, for the Christian, is the Spirit-examined life.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise."
verseByVerse.commentary: A man's response to praise reveals his character. The fool expands with praise and shrinks with criticism; the wise person holds both with equanimity, knowing that the LORD's evaluation is the only one that finally matters. Praise is more spiritually dangerous than adversity — adversity drives people to God, while praise tempts them toward self-sufficiency. This is why v.2 warns against self-promotion and why Paul could say he had "learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content" (Phil. 4:11) — the crucible of both suffering and praise had done its work.

27.theology:
Friendship as Means of Grace. Chapter 27 treats friendship as one of God's primary instruments for human formation. The friend who wounds faithfully (v.6), the counsel that gladdens (v.9), the iron sharpening iron (v.17) — these are not merely social goods but spiritual mechanisms. The Reformers called preaching, sacraments, and prayer the "means of grace"; Proverbs adds to this the faithful friend whose love is too serious to be merely pleasant. The church at its best is a community of faithful wounders.

Creatureliness and Humility. Verse 1 ("you do not know what a day may bring") and the closing pastoral image (vv.23–27) together present a vision of creaturely wisdom: know your limits, tend what is given, plan humbly. The theological virtue behind this is not pessimism but trust — trust in a God who holds the future and who is worthy to hold it. Christian hope does not eliminate planning; it transforms its spirit from grasping to stewardship.
27.examples:
Then: Proverbs' audience would have known the pastoral life intimately — flocks, herds, seasonal rhythms. The closing section (vv.23–27) is not romantic but practical: attend to what you have, do not speculate beyond your means, sustainable abundance is preferable to volatile wealth. The friendship section spoke to a culture where patronage and flattery were the social currency of court life; genuine friendship of the kind Proverbs describes was rare and precious precisely because it was so counter-cultural.

Now: Verse 17 (iron sharpens iron) is widely quoted in men's ministries and leadership circles — rightly so, though its cutting edge is often dulled into something merely motivational. The real application is uncomfortable: who in your life is allowed to wound you faithfully? Who will tell you what your spouse, your employees, and your therapist might not? The Christian who cannot answer that question is almost certainly growing softer, not sharper. And verse 1 is a direct rebuke of the five-year planning culture that imagines the future as essentially controllable — wisdom builds plans lightly held.

28.title: The Wicked Flee When No One Pursues
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion. <sup>5</sup>Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely. <sup>6</sup>Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. <sup>9</sup>If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. <sup>11</sup>A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out. <sup>13</sup>Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy. <sup>14</sup>Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity. <sup>20</sup>A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished. <sup>25</sup>A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched. <sup>27</sup>Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse.
28.overview:
Chapter 28 is one of Proverbs' most theologically concentrated chapters, weaving together themes of conscience, confession, justice, and integrity. The opening verse sets the tone: the wicked flee even when unpursued — they are haunted by a conscience that cannot be quieted. The righteous are bold as a lion — not because they are braver by temperament, but because they have nothing to hide before God.

The chapter's pastoral center is verse 13: "Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy." This is Proverbs' most direct statement about confession and forgiveness, and it anticipates the New Testament's fuller development: 1 John 1:9, the prodigal son, the ministry of reconciliation. Concealment breeds shame and shame breeds the restless flight of verse 1; confession brings the boldness that only forgiveness can give.

Keller identifies this chapter as showing that integrity is not merely an ethical preference but a structural feature of a well-ordered soul. The person of integrity is not trying to avoid getting caught; they have nothing to manage, because they live openly before God.

verseByVerse.quote: "The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion."
verseByVerse.commentary: The wicked person is haunted — by conscience, by memory, by the fear of exposure. They live in a state of low-grade anxiety that no external threat is required to produce. Augustine's "restless heart" applies here: the soul that has not found its rest in God will not find it in any other place, and the unconfessed sin becomes a permanent, nagging presence. The righteous person, by contrast, can be bold not because they are morally perfect but because they walk in the light, confessing and forsaking (v.13), with nothing hidden that needs protecting.

verseByVerse.quote: "Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways."
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs consistently refuses to equate wealth with blessing and poverty with curse. The person who is prosperous through crooked means has built their life on a foundation that will not hold — and their prosperity is a form of poverty because it is founded on the corruption of their soul. The poor man of integrity has what money cannot buy: a self that coheres, a face that can be shown. Jesus distills this: "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most important verses in Proverbs for Christian formation. Concealment is not merely ineffective — it is actively destructive, producing the restlessness of verse 1 and the hardened heart of verse 14. Confession is not therapeutic disclosure but covenantal honesty before God: naming what was done, without excuse or minimization. "Forsakes them" adds the crucial element: repentance is not mere regret but a change of direction. David's Psalm 32 is the poetic companion to this verse — the description of what concealment costs and what confession restores. The New Testament anchor is 1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins."

verseByVerse.quote: "Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity."
verseByVerse.commentary: The fear of the LORD is the posture of permanent openness before God — an ongoing sensitivity to his presence, his word, and his call. It is the opposite of the hardened heart, which is characterized by progressive insensitivity. Pharaoh is the great biblical paradigm: a heart that could have softened but, through repeated refusal, became incapable of softening. The Hebrew writer warns the same thing in the new covenant context: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts" (Heb. 3:7–8). Blessed is the soft heart — always aware of its need before God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse."
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs returns repeatedly to the economics of generosity: the one who gives to the poor enters a divine economy that operates by different laws than the zero-sum world assumes.
