"Will not want" is not a mechanical prosperity promise but a covenant assurance — the God who owns all things tends to the one who disperses freely. "Hides his eyes" is the posture of the person who has learned not to see need because seeing requires response. The hardened eye is the hardened heart applied to economics. Jesus saw Zacchaeus and the woman at the well and the blind beggar — he refused the hardened eye.

28.theology:
Conscience, Confession, and the Mercy of God. Verse 13 is Proverbs' most direct engagement with the mechanics of mercy. The theological claim is that God's mercy is available — "will obtain mercy" is not conditional on sinlessness but on confession and forsaking. This is not a works-righteousness framework but a grace framework: mercy is given freely to those who stop hiding. The gospel deepens and perfects this: the confession that obtains mercy is made to a God who has already borne the penalty in Christ. Confession is not appeasement; it is homecoming.

The Boldness of Integrity. Verse 1 presents courage not as a gift of temperament but as a fruit of character. The righteous person is bold as a lion because integrity creates a kind of structural fearlessness — nothing to hide, nothing to protect, no secret that could be exposed. This is the "freedom of a Christian" Luther described: the person who lives before God without pretense is free from the anxiety that haunts those who manage appearances. Paul could say "I am not ashamed of the gospel" (Rom. 1:16) because the gospel had done precisely this work in him.
28.examples:
Then: Ancient Israelite legal culture required witnesses and public testimony; concealment was a constant temptation in legal disputes, land transactions, and communal life. Verse 13 spoke into that culture's pressure to manage reputation through concealment rather than facing consequences through confession. The poor man of verse 6 would have been a recognizable figure: the day laborer with an unblemished reputation in a world where bribery and corruption were available to those with means.

Now: Verse 13 is the most directly applicable verse in this chapter for pastoral ministry. The epidemic of unconfessed sin — hidden addiction, secret financial failure, private moral collapse — produces precisely the restlessness of verse 1. The church that creates a culture of safe confession (not therapeutic oversharing, but covenant honesty) creates the conditions for the boldness of verse 1. And verse 27 ("hides his eyes") describes the posture of studied indifference to need — the averted gaze that has learned, through habit, not to see the homeless person on the corner, not to read the email from the struggling church, not to answer the call from the difficult family member.

29.title: Where There Is No Vision
29.text: <sup>1</sup>He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing. <sup>2</sup>When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan. <sup>7</sup>A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge. <sup>11</sup>A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back. <sup>12</sup>If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked. <sup>13</sup>The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. <sup>15</sup>The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. <sup>17</sup>Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart. <sup>18</sup>Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law. <sup>20</sup>Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. <sup>23</sup>One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor. <sup>25</sup>The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 gathers some of Proverbs' most quotable and weighty political and social wisdom, while returning constantly to the themes that have threaded through the whole book: the righteous vs. the wicked, the teachable vs. the stubborn, pride vs. humility. The famous verse 18 — "Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint" — is frequently misread as a vision-casting management principle, but its Hebrew context is far richer: without divine revelation, without the word of the LORD, human community loses its moral and social coherence.

The chapter also addresses the twin temptations of leadership: listening to falsehood (v.12) and the fear of man (v.25). The ruler who wants to be loved rather than just will tolerate flattery and generate corruption. The person who fears what others think becomes a snare to themselves — and a danger to those they lead. The antidote in both cases is the fear of the LORD, which is its own kind of freedom.

Keller reads verse 25 as one of Proverbs' most penetrating diagnoses of the human condition: the fear of man is not merely a social anxiety but a form of idolatry, a misplaced trust that enslaves precisely because it demands everything and delivers nothing lasting.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing."
verseByVerse.commentary: The stiff neck is one of the Bible's defining images of human rebellion — used of Israel repeatedly in the Pentateuch and by Stephen in Acts 7:51: "You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit." The person who resists correction again and again does not simply fail to improve; they harden into a condition where correction can no longer reach them. "Suddenly broken beyond healing" — the disaster arrives not as a warning but as a conclusion. The whole Proverbs book is a sustained argument that teachability is the foundation of wisdom. To refuse it is to choose a destination you cannot foresee from where you are standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan."
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs is not politically naive. It knows that leadership shapes culture — that the character of those who rule filters down through every institution and eventually reaches the ordinary person who simply wants to live and work in peace. The groan of the people under wicked rule is a moral indicator, not a mere political complaint. Christians vote, advocate, and serve in civic life precisely because they know that governance matters for human flourishing. The ultimate righteous ruler, of course, is the one whose kingship the prophets promised and Revelation celebrates: the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: "Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Prophetic vision" (chazon) is divine revelation — the word of the LORD given through his prophets. This is not a vision statement or a leadership philosophy; it is the Torah, the prophets, the whole counsel of God. Without it, communities lose the moral grammar that makes ordered life possible. The second half of the verse is equally important: the blessed person is the one who keeps the law — who has received divine revelation and lives within it. The New Testament fulfills this: the Spirit inscribes the law on the heart (Jer. 31:33; 2 Cor. 3:3), enabling the life that Proverbs commends not by external compulsion but internal transformation.

verseByVerse.quote: "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is Proverbs' version of the Magnificat: he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:51–52). Pride is structurally self-defeating: it positions you as the center of a universe that refuses to cooperate. The lowly in spirit — not the self-pitying or self-deprecating, but the genuinely humble — receives honor from a source that cannot be manufactured or gamed. Jesus embodies both halves: he humbled himself to the point of death, and God highly exalted him (Phil. 2:8–9). The Christian way of honor runs through the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe."
verseByVerse.commentary: The fear of man — caring more about what people think than about what God thinks — is one of the most pervasive and least-diagnosed spiritual disorders. It is a snare precisely because it is invisible: it operates through perfectly reasonable-sounding concerns about relationships, reputation, and social standing. Keller identifies it as a form of idolatry: the person who fears man has given to human opinion the authority that belongs to God alone. The antidote is trust in the LORD — not indifference to others, but a settled security in the one whose opinion is final. "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" (Ps. 27:1).

29.theology:
Revelation as Social Foundation. Verse 18 makes a claim that should trouble both secular and religious complacency: human society cannot sustain itself by human wisdom alone. It needs the word of God — not as a political imposition but as the moral grammar that makes community coherent. The history of every society that has tried to build order on human reason alone is the history of ideologies that eventually devour themselves. The church is, among other things, the community that keeps the word of God alive in the world — not for its own sake, but for the world's sake.

The Fear of the LORD vs. the Fear of Man. Verses 25 and 23 together present Proverbs' final pastoral diagnosis: pride (placing the self at the center) and fear of man (placing human opinion at the center) are two versions of the same disorder — life organized around anything other than the LORD. Both lead to a snare. Only trust in the LORD is safe, and only humility before the LORD leads to honor. This is the fear of the LORD in its final, practical form.
29.examples:
Then: The ruler who listens to falsehood (v.12) was an immediate practical concern in the ancient Near East — courtiers who told kings what they wanted to hear were a perennial danger, one that the prophets constantly opposed. The fear of man (v.25) was particularly acute for anyone in a patronage society: your livelihood, safety, and social standing all depended on powerful people's approval. Proverbs' call to trust the LORD rather than manage human opinion was countercultural in every ancient context.

Now: Verse 25 is the pastoral verse of the chapter — perhaps of the entire book — for contemporary application. The epidemic of anxiety, people-pleasing, cancel-culture terror, and social-media performance is Proverbs' "fear of man" writ large in digital ink. The pastor who preaches what the congregation wants to hear, the employee who never challenges injustice, the friend who flatters rather than wounds — all are in the snare. The antidote is not indifference but a stronger fear: the fear of the LORD that makes every other fear small.

30.title: The Words of Agur
30.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. <sup>2</sup>Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. <sup>3</sup>I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One. <sup>4</sup>Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know! <sup>5</sup>Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. <sup>6</sup>Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. <sup>7</sup>Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: <sup>8</sup>Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, <sup>9</sup>lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God. <sup>18</sup>Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: <sup>19</sup>the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin. <sup>24</sup>Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: <sup>25</sup>the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer.
30.overview:
Chapter 30 is the most distinctive unit in the book of Proverbs — the words of Agur son of Jakeh, an otherwise unknown figure whose opening confession is one of the most startling passages in wisdom literature. He begins not with a proverb but with an admission of total inadequacy: "I am too stupid to be a man. I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One" (vv.2–3). This is the fear of the LORD in its most radical form — a profound epistemic humility before the mystery of God.

The rhetorical questions of verse 4 — "Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists?" — echo God's speech from the whirlwind in Job 38–39 and anticipate the Prologue of John: the One who descended and ascended, who commands wind and wave, is the Son of God, the Word made flesh (John 3:13; Eph. 4:9–10). "What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!" is charged with irony — Agur does not know, but the reader of the whole canon does.

The prayer of verses 7–9 is one of the most theologically mature prayers in Scripture: give me neither poverty nor riches, only enough. It is the prayer of someone who understands the spiritual dangers of both extremes — the arrogance of abundance and the desperation of want. Keller calls it the perfect antidote to prosperity theology and poverty mysticism alike.

verseByVerse.quote: "Surely I am too stupid to be a man... Who has ascended to heaven and come down?... What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Agur's opening confession inverts every expectation. Wisdom literature claims to offer knowledge; Agur begins with an admission that he has none. This is not false modesty — it is the deepest wisdom: the recognition that the knowledge of God lies infinitely beyond human capacity. The rhetorical questions of verse 4 (ascending/descending, gathering wind, wrapping water) all describe the sovereign Creator. The closing question — "What is his son's name?" — has haunted interpreters throughout church history. Read in canonical fullness, it points unmistakably to the Son of God, the one who answers every question Agur could not (John 3:13; Col. 1:15–17). Proverbs 8's wisdom-figure has a name, and the New Testament gives it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar."
verseByVerse.commentary: After confessing his ignorance, Agur pivots to the one source of reliable knowledge: the word of God. "Proves true" — refined, tested, as precious metal is purified. God's word is not merely accurate but refined through the very fires of human history that test it. The command not to add (v.6) stands as a fence around revelation: the canon is given, not constructed. This anticipates Revelation 22:18–19, the New Testament's closing warning. Scripture's authority is grounded in the character of the One who spoke it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you... or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is perhaps the wisest prayer about money in all of Scripture. Agur understands what prosperity theology refuses to admit and poverty mysticism romanticizes: both extremes carry spiritual dangers. Abundance tempts toward self-sufficiency ("Who is the LORD?"); poverty tempts toward desperation and moral compromise. "Feed me with the food that is needful" echoes the manna in the wilderness (enough for each day) and anticipates the Lord's Prayer: "Give us this day our daily bread." The prayer is a confession that the right relationship to material things is dependence on God, not accumulation or renunciation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin."
verseByVerse.commentary: The numerical saying (three/four) is a characteristic form of ancient wisdom — the pattern creates a feeling of completeness that the final item disrupts or crowns. The four "ways" are all movements that leave no trace: the eagle, the serpent, the ship, the man. What Agur finds wonderful (pele) — the same word used for God's mighty acts — is the mystery of motion through a medium that closes behind it. The poem is a meditation on the limits of knowledge. There are things in creation — and supremely in human love — that cannot be fully comprehended, only reverently observed. Wisdom begins in wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: "Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer."
verseByVerse.commentary: The nature poems of chapter 30 (ants, coneys, locusts, lizards) recall Job 12:7: "Ask the beasts, and they will teach you." Wisdom is not only in the Torah and the sayings of the sages — it is inscribed in creation itself, available to those who pay attention. The ant teaches foresight without being lectured on it; the locust achieves coordination without a king. General revelation — God's wisdom embedded in the created order — is accessible to all who observe carefully. Special revelation perfects and redeems it; it does not abolish the wisdom of attentive creation-watching.

30.theology:
Agur's Confession and the Knowledge of God. Verses 2–4 present what theologians call the via negativa — the approach to God through what cannot be said rather than what can. Agur knows that the gap between human knowledge and divine reality is infinite. The only bridge is revelation — "every word of God proves true" (v.5). This epistemological structure is precisely what Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 1–2: human wisdom cannot know God; God reveals himself through the "foolishness" of the cross. The wise person is the one who, like Agur, knows what they do not know and receives what God has given.

Contentment as Theology. The prayer of verses 8–9 embodies what Paul calls "learned contentment" (Phil. 4:11). Contentment is not a natural temperament but a theological achievement — the fruit of trusting that God's provision, whatever its form, is sufficient. It requires a prior conviction about God's goodness and sovereignty that prosperity theology undermines and asceticism misunderstands. Agur's prayer is the wisest financial philosophy in Scripture: enough, by the hand of a good God.
30.examples:
Then: Agur's confession (vv.2–4) would have been startling in a culture of competing wisdom schools, each claiming to have the key to the good life. A sage who begins by confessing ignorance is subverting the genre from within. The numerical sayings (three things / four things) were a recognized teaching form — the pattern held attention and the final item delivered the punch. The prayer of vv.8–9 addressed a society in which both the prosperity of the few and the poverty of the many were daily realities.

Now: Agur's prayer (vv.8–9) is the most direct rebuke of the prosperity gospel available in the Old Testament — and it also rebukes the romanticization of poverty. "Give me neither" is the prayer of someone who has seen clearly what both do to the soul. In an age of financial anxiety and comparison culture, "feed me with the food that is needful for me" is a radical act of trust. And verse 4's cascading questions ("What is his name, and what is his son's name?") invite the reader who knows the New Testament to feel the full weight of the answer: the name that is above every name (Phil. 2:9).

31.title: The Excellent Wife
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him: <sup>2</sup>What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows? <sup>3</sup>Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings. <sup>4</sup>It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink, <sup>8</sup>Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. <sup>9</sup>Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy. <sup>10</sup>An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. <sup>11</sup>The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. <sup>20</sup>She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy. <sup>25</sup>Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. <sup>26</sup>She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. <sup>28</sup>Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: <sup>29</sup>"Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all." <sup>30</sup>Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. <sup>31</sup>Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
31.overview:
Chapter 31 is the crown of the book of Proverbs — and it is breathtaking in its literary architecture. The final poem (vv.10–31) is an acrostic: each verse begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to taw. The entire alphabet is enlisted to praise this woman. Nothing has been left out; she is the complete embodiment of wisdom.

The poem must be read in light of the whole book. Proverbs 1–9 introduced Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly as two great feminine figures calling to humanity. Lady Folly was seductive, loud, and ultimately fatal (ch.7). Lady Wisdom called from the heights, offered life, and pointed to the fear of the LORD (ch.8–9). Now, in the book's final movement, Lady Wisdom is embodied in a particular woman whose life is the concrete shape of wisdom incarnate: she fears the LORD (v.30), she opens her hand to the poor (v.20), she speaks with wisdom (v.26), she is clothed with strength and dignity (v.25).

This woman is not a job description for wives but a portrait of wisdom as it appears in an actual human life. She is also, for the Christian reader, a type of the church — the bride who fears the Lord, who does good rather than harm, who is praised at the gates. And she points ultimately to Christ himself, the Wisdom of God in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, who "surpasses them all" (v.29).

verseByVerse.quote: "Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy."
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the poem about the excellent wife, the chapter closes with a mother's instruction to her royal son: use your power to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves. This is Proverbs' political theology in two verses: power is given not to accumulate more but to serve those who have none. The king who does not defend the poor has misunderstood his calling entirely. This vision of power as advocacy reaches its fullest expression in the Lord Jesus, who "came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:45) — the ultimate advocate who pleads our cause before the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: "An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels... a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised."
verseByVerse.commentary: The poem opens with a rhetorical question — "who can find?" — that recalls Lady Wisdom's invitation in chapters 1–9 and the book of Job's meditation on hidden wisdom (Job 28). The answer here is: she is findable, she is real, she is here. The question is not her existence but the discernment to recognize and honor her. The crown of the portrait is verse 30: all her extraordinary competence, generosity, and strength flow from one source — the fear of the LORD. Remove that, and you have admirable competence; keep it, and you have wisdom embodied. This is the book's final answer to the question it began with in 1:7.

verseByVerse.quote: "She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy."
verseByVerse.commentary: Wisdom, in Proverbs, always has an economic dimension. The wise person is never indifferent to poverty. This woman's generosity is not an afterthought to her productivity but integral to it — she is a generator of abundance precisely so that she can distribute it. The open hand (v.20) is the image of a life that does not clutch its resources but moves them outward. The New Testament makes explicit what Proverbs implies: generosity is a theological act, not a social nicety. "Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD" (Prov. 19:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come."
verseByVerse.commentary: "She laughs at the time to come" — not because the future holds no difficulty but because she has laid provision for it and, more deeply, because she trusts the God who holds it. This is Proverbs' version of Agur's prayer: she does not fear the future because she has built her life on a foundation that the future cannot destroy. The eschatological laugh is the laugh of the woman in Psalm 46 whose city does not fall though the mountains be cast into the sea — and ultimately the laugh of the resurrection, where the last enemy has been defeated. "O death, where is your sting?" (1 Cor. 15:55).

verseByVerse.quote: "Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her... Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates."
verseByVerse.commentary: The poem ends at the gates — the place of public life, commerce, and justice where her husband is known (v.23) and where she herself is now praised. Her recognition is not manufactured; it is the natural overflow of a life well-lived. "Let her works praise her" — the testimony of a wise life is the life itself. The book of Proverbs closes not with a commandment but with an acclamation: this is what wisdom looks like in a human life, and it is beautiful. For the Christian, the portrait culminates in One who is himself the fullness of wisdom — who opened his hand for the poor, spoke with the teaching of kindness, laughed at death itself, and whose works praise him in the gates of the New Jerusalem.

31.theology:
Lady Wisdom Embodied. The structural genius of Proverbs is now fully visible: the book opens with a father urging his son to seek wisdom and avoid folly (chs.1–9), personified as two women. The book closes with wisdom embodied in a particular woman whose final credential is the fear of the LORD (v.30). The frame is complete. Lady Wisdom is not an abstraction; she is what a human life looks like when it is ordered toward God. For the Christian reader, Christ is the fullness of this embodiment: "Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1 Cor. 1:30).

The Fear of the LORD as Crown. Proverbs 1:7 begins: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Proverbs 31:30 ends: "a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised." The book is a vast unfolding of what lies between these two statements — the practical wisdom of a life lived in the fear of God. That fear is not dread but the relational posture of the creature before the Creator, the redeemed before the Redeemer. It issues in generosity, diligence, faithful speech, care for the poor, and the peculiar joy of the woman who laughs at the time to come. This is Proverbs' final word, and it is the beginning of the gospel.
31.examples:
Then: The acrostic form (aleph to taw) was a literary statement: this is everything, the complete alphabet of a wise life. Israelite readers would have recognized the woman of chapter 31 as the antithesis of Lady Folly (ch.7) and the embodiment of Lady Wisdom (ch.8). Her economic activity — buying fields, trading, making linen garments — was entirely realistic for a woman of means in the ancient Near East, where women managed households that were also small enterprises. Her praise "at the gates" was public honor in the place where civic life happened.

Now: Chapter 31 has sometimes been weaponized as a productivity checklist for Christian women. The poem resists this. It is not a job description but a portrait — and its crown is not efficiency but the fear of the LORD. Any reading that focuses on the woman's activities while ignoring verse 30 has misread the poem. More broadly, the chapter invites readers to ask: what does wisdom look like in a full, concrete human life? The answer is not a set of rules but a person — generously open-handed, dignified under pressure, laughing at the future, speaking with wisdom and kindness. The church is called to embody this portrait collectively: the community that fears the LORD, opens its hand to the poor, and lets its works praise it in the gates of the city it inhabits.

32.overview:
This commentary on Proverbs was prepared as a devotional and theological companion for personal and group study. It follows the same approach as the Isaiah, Ephesians, Acts, Ecclesiastes, Matthew, and John commentaries in this series: Reformed, evangelical, and doxological — written to glorify God and to help readers encounter the living Christ in the pages of Scripture.

The commentary draws especially on the work of Timothy Keller, whose God's Wisdom for Navigating Life (with Kathy Keller) and sermons on Proverbs model the approach taken here: wisdom not as moral self-improvement but as the reorientation of the whole person toward God, with Christ as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden. It also draws on the Reformed tradition as expressed by John Calvin, Derek Kidner, Bruce Waltke, Tremper Longman III, and Alistair Begg.
